# Part I: Discrete Filtering {.section-slide}

First definitions

## Signal and filters {.small-slide}

A **signal** is a sequence of real (or complex) number  $x(n)$ for all $n \in \ZZ$

::: {.notes}
In this course, a **signal** is a sequence of rear or complex numbers $x(n)$, efine for all times $n \in \ZZ$
:::

. . .

A linear and time invariance **filter** is a tranform which turns a signal into another

- $x(n)$ and $y(n)$ are the *input* and *output* respectively
- for any $m \in \ZZ$, the filter trasform $x(n-m)$ into $y(n-m)$

::: {.notes}
- A filter is a transform which turn s a signal into another signal, and which is both linear and invariant to translation.
- y and x are respectively the **output** and the **input** of the filter
- then for any integer $m$, the filter transform the translated version of the input into the translated version of the output
:::

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
All filters are characterize by **Impulse Response** $h(n)$, the trasform of the impulse signal $h(n) = \delta_0(n)$

**Convolution product** describes the relationship between input and output signals
$$
    y(n) = \sum_{m\in\ZZ} h(m) x(n - m)
$$
:::

::: {.notes}
- It can be porvode that all the filters are characterized by their **impulse response**, that is, the transform of the **impulse signal **$\delta_0$
- Then the general relationship between the input and the output signals is a **convolutional product** 
  - defined as the discrete integral envaluated for all values of shifts
- For the convolution product to be well defined, $h$ and $x$ need to satisfy some conditions:
  - the most common is the BIBO: bounded input $\implies$ bounded output
:::

::: {.column  width="35%"}

![](https://quincyaflint.weebly.com/uploads/2/6/5/0/26500868/convolution-1-fast_orig.gif){fig-align="center"}

:::

:::

## Fourier transforms {.small-slide}


Let $H(\eipiv)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ} h(n) e^{- 2 i \pi \nu n}$ and $X(\eipiv)=\sum_{n\in\ZZ} X(n) e^{- 2 i \pi \nu n}$ be the **Fourier transforms** of $h$ and $x$, reprectively, for all *normalized frequencies* $v\in\RR$

Then, the Fourier transform of the **Convolution product** $y$ is
$$
  Y(\eipiv) = H(\eipiv) X(\eipiv)
$$

The function $H(\eipiv)$ is called the **Frequency Response** of the filter

::: {.notes}
- Signals and filters are usually studied in the Fourier domain
- If both $h$ and $x$ have well-defined Fourier transform $H(\eipiv)$ and $X(\eipiv)$, where $\nu$ are the normalized frequencies
- then, the convolution product can be computed as direct producton of the Fourier transformes of the filetr and the input.
:::

## Causality and stability {.tiny-slide}

::: {.notes}
Beyond linearity and invariance to translation over time, we usually expect a filter to satisfy the following two conditions
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Causality

- Definition: $y(n)$ only depends on $x(k)$ , $k \leq n$
- Necessary and sufficient condition: $h(m)=0$ if $m<0$ (proof in the handout)
- Property: causal input $\implies$ causal output (proof in the handout)
- Remark: compulsory for real-time processing

::: {.notes}
- The causality is a compulsory condition when we need the filter to act in real-time.
- A filter is causal if and only if, for any input signal $x(n)$, the output $y(n)= (h \ast x)(n)$ only depend on the past sample of $x$, that is, $x(k)$, for $k \leq n$.
- Equivalently, causality is characterized by the necessary and sufficient condition that $h(n)$ is causal if and only if $h$ is zero for negative times.
- As a consequence, if both the impulse response and the input signal are causal, then the output is causal
:::

:::

::: {.fragment}
### (BIBO) Stability

- Definition: bounded input $\implies$ bounded output
- Necessary and sufficient condition $\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} | h(m) | < +\infty$ (i.e., $h \in l^1(\ZZ)$)
- Property: filter's frequency response is continuous (proof in the notes)
- Remark: this is numerically compulsory
  - If $x_q = x + e$, then $y_q = y + h\ast e$
  - If $h\in l^1(\ZZ)$, $\| h \ast e \|_{\infty} \leq \|h\|_1 \|e\|_\infty$, otherwise $h\ast e$ may diverge

::: {.notes}
- Next, the **stability** condition is **always** required whenever we want to numerically compute the output
- The stability is defined as: a filter is stable if and only if, for any bounded input $x$, the output is also bounded
- This is also called as BIBO (bounded input bounded output)
- and this translated to the necessary and sufficient condition that the l1-norm of the filter is finite.
- As a consequence, the frequency response of a stable filter is always continuous
  - in fact, assume for instance that we have an input $x$ corrupted by some quantization noise $e$, due to rounding errors
  - then, by applying the filter $h$ to $x_q$, we get the output $y_q = y + h \ast e$,
  - if the filter is stable, then the residual part is bounded.
:::

:::

## Ideal filters {.small-slide}

<!-- ### Ideal filter
- selects the band-pass of the inputs
- rejects all other frequencies (in the stop-band) -->

::: {.notes}
- An ideal filter selects a given frequency range called band-pass of the input
- and rejects all other frequencies, which form the stop-band
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Low pass filter (periodic spectrum)

- Frequency response: $H(e^{2i\pi \nu}) = \begin{cases} 1 &\mbox{if } |\nu| < \nu_c \\ 0 &\mbox{if } |\nu| > \nu_c \end{cases}$
- Impulse response: $h(n) = 2 \nu_c \sinc(2\pi \nu_c n)$

::: {.notes}
- the pass-band of a ideal low-pass filter constains all frequencies lower than a given threshold, called **cut-off frequency**
- By applying the inverse DTFT to the filter, we obtain the impulse response of the filter, which is availabe in closed form, that is, a scaled sinus cardinal
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Exercise: band-pass filter

- Frequency response: $H(e^{2i\pi \nu}) = \begin{cases} 1 &\mbox{if } ||\nu|-\nu_0| < \nu_c \\ 0 &\mbox{if } ||\nu|-\nu_0| > \nu_c \end{cases}$
- Impulse response: $h(n)=4 \nu_c \sinc(2 \pi \nu_c n) \cos(2 \pi \nu_0 n)$

::: {.notes}
- The ideal band-pass filteris is then characterized by two parameters, a **central frequency** $\nu_0$ and a **bandwidth** of $2\nu_c$. 
- A band-pass can be built by the differences of 2 low-pass filters and its impulse response can be easily computed in closed-form resulting in a modulated sinus cardinal
:::

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}
::: {.center}
[Causality? Stability?]{.alert}
:::

::: {.notes}
- For the low-pass filter, we know that the sinus cardianl is not causal and not stable (l1-norm is infinity)
  - we do not need to calculate it, just checking the frequency response:
    - it is even and real: then it cannot be causal
    - it is discontinuous: then it cannot be stable
- For the band-pass filter, it is neither causal nor stable, as the same reasons apply
:::
:::

## Transient and steady states {.tiny-slide}

::: {.notes}
- When a causal filter is applied to a causal input signal, we can define two regimes: 
- a transient state and a steady state
:::


::: {.fragment}
For example

- $x(n)$ is a unit step signal: $x(n) = \vbone_{[0,+\infty[}(n)$
- $h(n)$ is an averaging filter: $h(n) = \frac1N \vbone_{[0,N-1[}(n)$

::: {.notes}
- Let s assume that the input signal is the unit step signal
- and we consider the causal averaging filter of length $N$ sample
- From before, we know that that the output signal is causal, because both h and x are.
  - we would expect that averaging a constant signal like the step unit would produce $y(n)=1$ for positive samples.
:::
:::

. . . 

We observe

- From $n=0$ to $N-2$: transient state $\quad\to$ ramp
- From $n=N-1$ to $+\infty$: steady state $\quad\to$ constant signal


::: {.notes}
- Actually this happens only after $N-1$ taps, that is the lenght of the filter.
- The interval between 0 and N-2 looks like a ramp and goes from 0 to 1.
- This transition is called the **transient state** of the filter, which is followed by the **steady state** of the filter, where the output converge to the expected state
:::

![Transient and steady states of a causal filter](../notebooks/images/cm01_transient_steady_state.svg){fig-align="center" width=80%}

## Phase and group delays {.tiny-slide}

Frequency response: $H(\eipiv)=H_R(\nu) e^{i \phi(\nu)}$

::: {.notes}
- Let s consider the polar factorization of the frequency response of the filter $H(\eipiv)$ into real amplitude $H_R$ and phase $\phi(\nu)$.  
:::

. . . 

Phase and group delays:
<!-- [More about [Group and Phase delays](https://www.merlijnvanveen.nl/en/study-hall/165-group-delay-101)] -->

$$
\begin{cases}
  \taup(\nu_0) &= - \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{\phi(\nu_0)}{\nu_0}\\
  \taug(\nu_0) &= - \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{d \phi}{d \nu}{\nu_0}
\end{cases}
$$

::: {.notes}
- We will here define two quantities that measure the delays (in unit of time) that different frequencies components expericey as they pass through a filter.
- This delays may be frequency dependent, so that the output signal may experience distortions 
- the phase delay is the time delay experienced by an individual sinuoidal frequency component
- the group delay is the time delay experienced by the overall envolop or "group" of frequencies
:::

. . .

Frequency response in the neighborhood of $\nu_0$ (proof in the notes):

$$
  H(\eipiv) \simeq H_R(\nu_0) e^{- i 2 \pi (\nu_0 \taup(\nu_0) + (\nu - \nu_0) \taug(\nu_0))}
$$

::: {.notes}
- In order to explain these definition, let us study the filter response in the neighborhood of the frequency $\nu_0$
- Then, the filter response can be approximated using the two quantities.
- And it is easy to see by developing the Taylor expansion (let s do it)
:::

. . .


Filtering of a *narrowband* signal $x$ ($y = h \ast x)$ (proof in the notes):
$$
  \underbrace{x(n) = a(n) e^{i 2 \pi \nu_0 n}}_{X(\eipiv)= A\left(e^{2 i \pi (\nu - \nu_0)}\right)} \quad\implies\quad y(n) \simeq H_R(\nu_0) a(n - \taug(\nu)) e^{i 2 \pi \nu_0(n - \taup(\nu_0))}
$$

::: {.notes}
- Let us now consider the output signal $y$ resulting from the convolution of $h$ with a narrow-band signal $x$.
- Remeber that a narrowband signal is a signal $x(n)$ 
  - that results from the multiplication of temporal envelop modulated by a carrier frequency 
  - and the amplitude is assumed to be limited to the neighthood of the zero frequency
- Let us develop the math for this ...
- This proves that the output is also a narrowband signal, of same carrier frequency $\nu_0$ as $x(n)$,
  - with temporal envolop which is shifted by the group delay $\taug$ w.r.t. to $x$
  - and initial phase shifet by the phase delay $\taup$ w.r.t. $x(n)$
:::

. . .

Linear phase filters (= the delay is constant)

::: {.notes}
- As final remarks, notice that the temporal wavefrom of the input $x$ is not distorted by the filter, if and only if the group and phase delays are equal.
- This necessary and sufficient condition for this is that $h$ is a **linear phase filter**

:::

# Part II - Z-transform {.section-slide}

##  Z-transform {.tiny-slide}

Definition: $H(z) = \sum_{n = -\infty}^{+\infty} h(n) z^{-n}$, called the **Transfer function**

- From the DTFT $H(\eipiv) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h(n) e^{- 2 i \pi \nu n}$, we use $z = e^{i\pi \nu} \in \CC$

::: {.notes}
- The Z-transform is a very powerfool tool to characterize the properties of discrete filters
- The Z-transform can be derived from the definition of the DTFT, by introducting the complex number $z$.
- Why can't we just use the DTF?
  - The DFT assume an integer number of samples, defined over a cicle, a period
  - We can have filters that have infinite impulse responses, for which we cannot define a finite number of sample
  - so the Z-transform is like the DFT, but under the assumption of silence after N sampels, rather than infinite repetition
:::

. . .

Domain of convergence: $\calD = \{ z \in \CC / \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} |h(n)| |z|^{-n} < + \infty \}$ with shapes:

::: {.notes}
- The domain of convergence for the Z-trasform is related to the characteristics of the filters
- In the general cases, it looks like a ring, that is the intersection of two disks
:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

- in the general case:** $\calD$ is a ring (or $\emptyset$)

::: {.incremental}
- if FIR filters: $\calD = \CC \setminus 0$
- if anti-causality: $\calD$ is a disk
- if **causality:** $\calD$ is the complement of a disk

::: {.notes}
- Then if the filter are FIR, the domain span the entire complex plane, without the origin
- if the filter is anti-causal, the domain is shaped like a disk
- and finally if causal, it the complement of the disk.
:::
::: 

:::

::: {.column}

![Z-transform](https://www.oreilly.com/api/v2/epubs/urn:orm:book:9781118393956/files/OEBPS/images/nbapp03f003.jpg){width=70%}

:::

:::


## Basic properties {.small-slide}

**Stability:** the ring $\calD$ contains the unit circle
  
  - The ZT matches the DTFT on the unit circle

::: {.notes}
- We can easily prove that $h$ is stable if and only if the ring $\calD$ contains the unit circle.
- It can be derived by applying the definition $\sum_{n\in\ZZ} | h(n) | < + \infty$ that implies $z=1$
:::

. . .

Linearity: $a_1 h_1 + a_2 h_2 \to a_1 H_1 + a_2 H_2$ with ($\calD \supset \calD_1 \supset \calD_2$)


::: {.notes}
- Then, we have a set properties that are similar to the one of the DTFT
- we have the linearity of the tranformation
:::


. . .

Delay: $y(n) = x(n-k) \iff Y(n)=z^{-k} X(z)$


::: {.notes}

- Applying a delay is equal to multiply by $z^{-k}$

:::


. . .

Convolution product:

  - if $y = h\ast x$, then $Y(z)=H(z)X(z)$, $\calD_y \supset \calD_h \cap \calD_x$


::: {.notes}

We can compute the convolution products, translates into a product in the transformed domain

:::

. . .

Insertion of zeros: $Y(z) = X(z^L) \iff y(nL) = x(n)$, $y=0$ elsewere


::: {.notes}
Then, adding zeros between consecutives samples, doesn't change the signal content: the specturm is squeeze and repeated.
:::

. . .

Inverse filter

  - if $h \ast h_i = \delta$, then $H(z)H_i(z) = 1$ for $z \in \calD_h \cap \calD_{h_i}$


::: {.notes}

Finally, as consequence of the convolution product, the inverse filter, is the one that results in the identity when the two transform are multiplied.

:::


## Example of ZT {.small-slide}


::: {.notes}

Here are a few example of useful Z-transforms.

We have:

- the identity filters
- the step filter
- the rectangular filter, that is, the ideal low-pass filter

:::

- $h(n) = \delta(n)$ $\implies$ $H(z) = 1$, $\quad\forall z \in \CC$
- $h(n) = 1_{[0,+\infty[}(n)$ $\implies$ $H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z^{-1}}$, $\quad\forall |z| > 1$
- $h(n) = 1_{[0,\ldots,N-1[}(n) \implies H(z) = \frac{1 - z^{-N}}{1 - z^{-1}}$, $\quad\forall |z| \neq 0$

. . .


AR1 filter:

  - $h(n) = \begin{cases}a^n &\text{if } n\geq 0 \\ 0 &\text{if } n < 0\end{cases} \implies H(z)= \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}}$ with $\calD = \{ z \in \CC / |z| > |a|\}$
  

::: {.notes}
The autoregression filter of order 1 (also know as AR1 filter) is importat filter that we will later define a **recursive filter**

- Let be $h(n)$ defined as $a^n$ for positive samples and zeros otherwise
- The impulse response is causal, so we already know that the domain of convergence is the complement of a disk, which can be proove to be of radius $a$
- Note that, the filter is stable $\iff$ the domain contains the unit cirle, that is, $|a| < 1$. 
- Which makes sense, as for $|a| < 1$ the series converge

:::

. . . 

- $h(n) = \begin{cases}-a^n &\text{if } n< 0 \\ 0 &\text{if } n \geq 0\end{cases} \implies H(z)= \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}}$  with $\calD = \{ z \in \CC / |z| < |a|\}$
  

::: {.notes}

Then we have the **anti-causal** version, defined similarly, but with a negative coefficiens and for negative samples

- we can notice that the form of the Z-tranform is the same
- but the domain of converges is different, which is now the interior of the disk with radious $a$
:::

## Autoregressive filter of order 1 {.center .small-slide}

::: {.callout}
## Autoregression filter of order 1

- Transfer function: $H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - a z^{-1}}$
- Input/output relationship : $y(n) - a y(n-1) = x(n)$

:::


::: {.notes}

- Since the causal and anti-causal AR1 filter have the same transfer function, 
- then we have two **implementations** of the same filter
- which in the time domain can be written in a recursive way as here
- in an equation that is called **input/output relationship**
:::

. . .

|                             |       Forward recursion       |   Backward recursion              |
|-----------------------------|:-----------------------------:|:---------------------------------:|
| Implementation              | $y(n)=a y(n-1) + x(n)$        | $y(n)= \frac{y(n+1) + x(n+1)}{a}$ |
| IR ($x(n)=\delta_0(n)$)     | $h(n) = a^n \vbone_{\{n\geq 0\}}$  | $h(n) = a^n \vbone_{\{n\geq 0\}}$      |
| Domain                      | $\{ z \in \CC / |z| < |a| \}$ | $\{ z \in \CC / |z| < |a| \}$     |
| Properties                  | causal , stable if $|a| < 1$  | anti-causal, stable if $|a| > 1$  |


::: {.notes}

The forward recursion is defined for increasing times

- this is the causal implementation
- and it is numarecally stable if and only if $|a|<1$
- that is, any error in the computation of $y(n-1)$ is reduced by a factor $|a|$ in the computation of $y(n)$

The backward recursion, or anticausal implementation, defined instead for decreasing times

- it is numerically stable if and only if $|a|>1$,
- since any error in the computation of $y(n+1)$ is reduced by a factor 1 over $|a|$ in $y(n)$

:::

. . .


::: {.notes}

In this simple case, looking at $a$ is sufficient to know which implementation.

But this will be now generalized to the general context of **recursive filters**

:::


# Parte III - Recursive filters {.section-slide}

## Recursive filters {.small-slide}

Input-output relationship

$$
\sum_{k=0}^N a_k y(n-k) = \sum_{k=0}^M b_k x(n - k)
$$


::: {.notes}

Recursive filters generalize the notion of AR1 filter of the previous slides

The I/0 relationship relates the samples of both the output signal $y$ and the input signal $x$
:::

. . .

Computation of the output (causal implementation)
$$
y(n) = \frac{1}{a_0} \left[  \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x(n - k) - \sum_{k=1}^N a_k y(n - k) \right]
$$


::: {.notes}

Note that this relation defines a filter 

- where the output sampes are linear function of the input samples
- delaying the input signal is equivalent to delaying the output signal by the same delay

Therefore we can define an impulse response whose impulse response looks like this.

The I/0 relationship admits several implementation

- this one is the causal one

:::

. . .

Transfer function

$$
  H(z) 
    = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^M b_k z^{-k}}{\sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^{-k}}
    = \frac{b_0}{a_0} \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})}
$$


::: {.notes}

Contrary to the impulse response, the transfer function can be always expressed as a simple function of the coefficients $a_k$ and $b_k$ as shown here

- where $c_k$ are known as the **zeros** and the $d_k$ are known as the **poles** of the filter.

:::


## Example of recursive filters {.small-slide}

### Auto-regression filters (if $M=0$, AR of order $N$)

$$
  y(n) = \frac{b_0}{a_0} x(n) - \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{a_k}{a_0} y(n - k)
$$

### Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters

- If $N=0$, FIR filter of length $M$
  $$
    h(n) = \begin{cases} \frac{b_n}{a_0} &\text{if } n=0,\ldots,M\\ 0 &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
  $$
- Casual filters, uncoditionally stable
- If the IR is symmentric or anti-symmetric, the phase is linear


::: {.notes}

There are two particular classes of recursive filters which are widely used in signal processing 

- the AR filters
- and the Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters

The AR filters, are recursive with no zeros 

- The I/0 relationship simplifies to this formulation
- This filters are widely used in speech processing, because they can model the physical model of the vocal track

The FIR filters are recursive filters with no pole

- their impulse response can be simply written as this
- they are widely used in signal processing, because they are stable and causal by construction
- in addition, if the IR is symmetric (or anti-symmetric), their phase is linear (which will be proved in the next lecture)
:::

## Recursive filters {.small-slide}

### Transfer function of a recursive filter
$$
  H(z) 
    = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^M b_k z^{-k}}{\sum_{k=0}^N a_k z^{-k}}
    = \frac{b_0}{a_0} \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})}
$$

Domain of convergence: $\calD$ is a ring bounded by 2 poles, with no pole inside of it

- **Stable** filter $\to$ $\calD$ is the largest ring containing the unit circle and no pole
- **Stable and causal** filters $\to$ whose poles are all strictly inside the unit circle
- if the $a_k$ and $b_k$ are real, the poles and zeros are either real, or form conjugate pairs


::: {.notes}

The transfer function of a recursive filter tells us some properties of of the domain of convengence of the filter

- the domain $\calD$ is a ring, bounded by two poles, with no pole inside
- there is an **unique stable** implementation if and only if there is no pole on the unit circle
- there is a **unique stable and causal** implementation if and only if all polse are strictly inside the unit circle
- if all the coefficients $a_k$ and $b_k$ are real, the poles and zeros are either real, or form conjgate pairs

:::

::: {.notes}

Suggested visualization:

- 2 poles inside the circle $\to$ only the outer ring contains the unit circle
- Push $d_2$ past 1 $\to$ now the middle ring is the stable one
  - only the mixed implementation is stable
  - stability and causality are separate 
- Push both poles outside (1.4, 1.6) $\to$  the inner circle becomes stable
  - the filter is purerly anti-causal
  - stability is not only "decaying"
- slide $d_2$ toward 0.1 $\to$ tje middle ring collapses onto the unit circle 
  - no ring contains it
- make a pole negative (-0.8) $\to$ this make alternative impulse response
  - a pole near z=-1 make a resonance at the nyquits frequency


:::


## Computation of the IR from the ZT {.tiny-slide .scrollable}


::: {.notes}

In this slide we recall the methodology to compute the impulse response from the Z-transform

:::

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
\

$H(z) = \frac{1}{1 - \frac52 z^{-1}  + z^{-2}}$
:::

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
1. If necessary, extract from $H(z)$ a term in $z^n$, so that numerator and denominator only contain negative powers of $z$ plus a constant

Nothing to extract: already a ratio in $z^{-n}$
:::

. . . 

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
1. Factorize the numerator and denominator as product of monomials of $z^{-1}$

$H(z) = \frac{1}{(1 - 2z^{-1})(1 - \tfrac12 z^{-1})}$
:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
3. Compute the partial fraction decomposition of $H(z)$ as a function of $z^{-1}$

$H(z) = \frac{4/3}{1-2z^{-1}} - \frac{1/3}{1-\frac12 z^{-1}}$
:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
::: {}
4. Expansion this fractions in power series

  - of $z^{-1}$ if we compute the causal IR, of if we compute the stable IR and if the pole is inside the unit circle
  - of $z$ if we compute the *anti*-causal IR, or if we compute the stable and if the pole is outside of the unit circle 
:::

::: {.small}
ROC: $\tfrac12 < |z| < 2$:

$\frac{1}{1-\tfrac12 z^{-1}} = \sum_{n\ge 0} 2^{-n} z^{-n}$

$\frac{1}{1-2z^{-1}} = -\sum_{n\ge 1} 2^{-n} z^{n}$
::: 

:::

. . .

::: {layout=[3,2] .small}
5. Identify the resulting expression with $H(z) = \sum_{n\in \ZZ} h(n)z^{-n}$


::: {.small}
$h(n) = \begin{cases}\frac23 (\frac12)^{n+1} - \frac23 2^{n+1} &n \ge 0\\0 & \text{else}\end{cases}$ 
:::
:::

## Geometric interpretation of the FR {.small-slide}

### Example (AR2 filter):
$$
H(z) = \frac1{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}} = \frac1{(1 - p z^{-1}) (1 - p^\ast z^{-1})}
$$


::: {.notes}

The shape of the Frequency response of a recursive filter can be easily deduced from the expansion of its transfer function.

Lets consider this, the causal AR2 filter, where we assume the coefficients form two poles in a conjugate pair.

:::

. . .

<br>

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

$$
\begin{align}
  |H(z)| &= \frac1{PM \times QM} \\
  \arg H(z) &= 2 \arg(OM) \\
            &\quad- \arg(PM) - \arg(QM)
\end{align}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

<iframe src="widgets/cm01_geometric_fr.html" width="100%" height="380"
        style="border:none;" loading="lazy"></iframe>

:::

:::

::: {.notes}

Let

- M be the coordinate of the point in the Z-plane representing the complex number $z$
- P be the point for $p$
- and Q the point of the conjugate $p$

Then PM and QM are the distances between these two points

Applying the equation $z=\eipiv$, we can plot the magnitude of the frequency response $|H(\eipiv)|$

Moving $\nu$ from 0 to $\frac12$, M travel over the unit cicle counter-clockwise, from 1 to 1

When M is close to P, the distance PM is small, then the magnitude of $H(z)$ is high, producting a resonance peak.

:::

## Spectral factorization {.small-slide .blurred}

Factorization of the transfer function

$$
  H(z) 
    = \frac{b_0}{a_0} \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})}
$$

Amplitude respense ($z = \eipiv)$

$$
  | H(\eipiv) |^2 = H(z) H(1/z^\ast) 
    = \left| \frac{b_0}{a_0} \right|^2 \frac{\prod_{k=1}^M  (1 - c_k z^{-1})(1 - c_k^\ast z^{-1})}{ \prod_{k=1}^N (1 - d_k z^{-1})(1 - d_k^\ast z^{-1})}
$$

- Poles of $|z| < 1$: stability + causality
- Zeros of $|z| < 1$: minimal phase 

## All-pass filters {.small-slide .blurred}

Definition: $H(z) = \prod_{k=1}^N \frac{z^{-1} - c_k^\ast}{1 - c_k z^{-1}}$ where $| c_k | < 1$ $\forall k$

$H(z)$ is all-pass, *causal* and stable

Properties (if $y = h \ast x$):

- $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} | x(n) |^2 = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} | y(n) |^2$
- An all-pass filter is such that $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{N} |x(n)|^2 \geq \sum_{n=-\infty}^{N} |y(n)|^2$  
  Proof hint: $x_N(n) = x(n) \times  1_{]-\infty, N]}(n)$

## Spectral factorization {.small-slide .blurred}

![](images/fig9.svg)

## Minimal phase filters {.small-slide .blurred}

- Definition: filter whose poles and zeros are all inside the unit circle
- Any causal and stable recursive filter is the product of all-pass filter and a minimal phase filter
- Properties (if $g$ is causal and stable, $y = g \ast x$ and $|G| = |G_m|$)
  - The inverse filter is also stable and causal
  - $\sum_{n = -\infty}^{+\infty} | y(n) |^2 \geq \sum_{n=-\infty}^N |y(n)|^2$
  - $g_m$ has the lowest group delay

# Part IV - FIR filters: window method {.section-slide}

## Window methods {.tiny-slide}

**Example:** FIR of the ideal low-pass filter $h(n)= 2 \nu_c \sinc(2 \nu_c n)$

- The respense is IIR, non-causal, non-stable

::: {layout="[100,-20,100]" layout-valign="center"}

![](./images/fig39.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="right"}

![](./images/fig38.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="left"}

:::

  
::: {.notes}

Let us consider an ideal low pass filter

which has a flat response between to cut off frequencies $\pm \nu_c$

The impulse response is known in closed form, and we know that it is infinite, non-causal and non-stable

We can built a **finite** impulse response by multiplying this by a window with finite temporal support, in the time domain

We then obtain an FIR filter, that we can make causal applying a temporal shift

:::


. . . 

Synthesis of a Type I causal FIR filter

- Trunctaion and temporal shift

::: {layout="[100,-20,100]" layout-valign="center"}

![](./images/fig40.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="right"}

![](./images/fig41.svg){style="height:120px" fig-align="left"}

:::


::: {.notes}

The spectar result is a convolution of the Fourier transform of the ideal response and the Fourier transform of the window

And in the figure we can see the impulse and frequency response of the FIR filter synthetised by the window method

:::


## Gibbs phenonemon {.small-slide}

::: {.r-stack}

![](images/fig42.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig43.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig46.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig47.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig48.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig49.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig50.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

![](images/fig51.svg){width=50% .fragment fig-align="center"}

:::

::: {.notes}

We can notice two effects

- **ripples** appear in the passband and in the stopband, which are related to the sidelobes of the Fourier transform of the window.
  - this means that teh **stopband attenation** is related to the **level of this sidelobes**
- the obtained filter is no longer infinitely selective: 
  - a **transition band** appears between the passbass and the stopband. 
    - the width of this transition band (that is the **filter selectivity**) are related to the **width** of the **main lobe** of the transform of the window
:::


## Choice of a suitable window {.small-slide}

::: {.notes}

The selection of the window's shappe is based on a trade-off between the level of the sideloble and the width of the main lobes.

Here we can compare different windows that are used in signal processing

:::

$$
  h(n) = 2 \nu_c \sinc(2 \nu_c n) w(n)
$$

where $w(n)$ is a symmetric window of a finite support

![](images/fig53.svg){width=50% fig-align="center"}


## Notable windows {.small-slide}


::: {.panel-tabset}
## [Rectangular window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = \vbone_{[0,P-1]}(n)
$$

- width: $\frac{2}{P}$
- second lobe: -13 dB
- decrease rate: -6 dB / octave

:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig16.svg)

:::

:::

## [Barlett window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column .small}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = 1 - \left| \frac{2n}{P-1} - 1 \right|
$$

- width: $\frac4P$
- second lobe: -26 dB
- decrease rate: -12 dB / octave

:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig17.svg)

:::

:::

## [Hann window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = 0.5 - 0.5 \cos \left( 2 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right)
$$

- width: $\frac4P$
- second lobe: -26 dB
- decrease rate: -12 dB / octave

:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig18.svg)

:::

:::

## [Hamming window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>
$$
  w(n) = 0.54 - 0.46 \cos \left( 2 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right)
$$

- width: $\frac4P$
- second lobe: -41 dB
- decrease rate: -6 dB / octave
:::

::: {.column}

![Hamming window](images/fig19.svg)

::: 

:::

## [Blackman window]{.small}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}
<br>

::: {.small}
$$
  w(n) = 0.4266 - 0.4965 \cos\left( 2 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right) + 0.076  \cos \left( 4 \pi \frac{n}{P-1} \right)
$$
:::



- width: $\frac6P$
- second lobe: -57 dB
- decrease rate: -18 dB / octave
:::

::: {.column}

![](images/fig20.svg)

::: 

:::

:::

## Window method {.small-slide}


### Advantages

- Stability, causality
- Linear phase filter if symmetric window

### Drawbacks

- the transition bands are widened
- the spurious ripples
  - are due to side lobes
  - do not have a constant amplitude
  - are the same in passband and stopband
